newsitem.title: UK: Italian, Spanish bond markets still attractive.
newsitem.headline: Italian, Spanish bond markets still attractive.

text.p: Italy and Spain's high-yielding bond markets look set to keep luring investors for a while after both broke spread records versus German Bunds on Wednesday, analysts said.
"I'd have a go at both of them," enthused Vaughan Hobbs, European bond trader at Societe Generale in London, when asked whether he preferred Italian BTPs or Spanish Bonos after their latest advance.

Buoyed by favourable economic data and expected interest rate cuts, the spread gap against Germany narrowed to a record 90 basis points for Spain and 150 basis points the case of Italy. By 1410 GMT, they had eased to 96 and 157 basis points respectively.

"I would not be surprised to see a bit of consolidation into the end of the week, but it won't last very long because people who misssed the boat are going to want to jump in and will see that as an opportunity," Hobbs said.

He said it would make sense to view any bout of profit-taking as a buying opportunity with the market seeing scope for the spreads to melt all the way down to 75 basis points for Spain and 135 basis points for Italy.

Elisabeth Afseth of fixed income sales at Williams de Broe said Spain was the more attractive of the two countries since it was likelier to qualify for the first round of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) than debt-laden Italy.
She said investors should consider five-year Spanish paper as the short end already priced in early rate cuts, while the long end might not have much further to go against Germany.

The March contract on 10-year Spanish bond futures was at 113.87, down 32 basis points on the day, after setting a contract high of 114.65 earlier in the session. The cash bond was up 16 basis points at 113.96, yielding 6.716 percent.
March BTPs stood at 130.73, eight basis points up, while cash bonds were up 42 basis points at 110.40, yielding 7.334 percent.
Afseth said a spread of just over 100 basis points would look more reasonable for Bonos than the 90 region.
"There is such a positive market view on Bonos the spread might stay tight for a bit but eventually widen," she said.

Afseth said a half-point could come off Italian interest rates in the next month. But while weak economic growth would help this to happen it would at the same time make it harder to meet the Maastricht treaty criteria for EMU.
Hobbs said a rate cut of quarter to half of a percentage point would spark some profit-taking and the spread could widen a little -- as it could if the rate cut did not happen yet.
"If they hold off, they maintain the credibility of not being seen to rush in and cut rates too early. And people will still be waiting for that cut," he said.
Hobbs said he preferred the 10-year sector because the short end had discounted most of the good news.
Peter Osler, head of research at GNI, said there was still scope for the Italian yield spread versus Germany to narrow further before it widened again.
Economic fundamentals were all pointing in a bond-friendly direction, including year-on-year industrial output for November which fell 5.9 percent against a forecast of a 4.1 percent fall.
Osler said investors should stick to liquid areas at the long end of the market as they sought to take advantage of whatever upward scope remained for BTPs.

"I wouldn't want to chase BTPs too much further because there is always the prospect of something going wrong with EMU, so in the longer term that spread obviously can widen a lot farther than it can narrow."
